name: Hindutva
summary: Hindutva, as V. D. Savarkar defined it in 1923, makes the Hindu people the Indian nation: those for whom the land from the Indus to the seas is both fatherland and holy land, bound by common blood and culture. M. S. Golwalkar, long-time head of the RSS, developed it into a doctrine of Hindu Rashtra: a unitary state, assimilation of Muslims and Christians into the national culture, protection of the cow, a ban on conversion and rejection of Western secularism, socialism and communism.
scope: The canonical core: Savarkar's Essentials of Hindutva (1923) and Golwalkar's We, or Our Nationhood Defined (1939) and Bunch of Thoughts (1966, the RSS head's mature statement, including his memorandum on national integration), with Jaffrelot's scholarship. Golwalkar's 1966 positions are used where they differ from the 1939 text. Deendayal Upadhyaya's Integral Humanism could not be opened in full text and is not used. The BJP's government programme is a carrying party's and is excluded. Hindu nationalism and Hinduism as a religion have their own entries. Strict strand rule: a position stated only by Golwalkar is null unless Savarkar or an RSS Pratinidhi Sabha resolution also states it. RSS resolutions on conversion, cow protection and the unitary state could not be found on rss.org.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Savarkar's Essentials makes a shared Hindu culture and history one of the three bonds of the nation, and Golwalkar's Bunch of Thoughts builds the whole case for Hindu Rashtra on guarding the nation's inherited way of life.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Savarkar traces the Hindu people unbroken from the Vedic Sapta Sindhu to the present, and Golwalkar's Bunch of Thoughts describes the same nation as continuous from ancient times.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Savarkar defines the Hindu by a land that is both fatherland (pitribhu) and holy land (punyabhu), and Golwalkar calls Bharat a Dharmabhoomi and Punyabhoomi whose mutilation no son can accept; Jaffrelot documents the same land-centred doctrine.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Savarkar says Hindus, whose past, present and future are bound to the land as fatherland and holy land, are the bedrock of the Indian state, and Golwalkar's Bunch of Thoughts rests Hindu Rashtra on the same tie to the soil.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Savarkar bases Hindutva on common blood, culture and land and calls the Hindus a race-nation, and Golwalkar's We (1939) uses the same 'Hindu race' idea; the 1966 Bunch of Thoughts lets others merge into the nation by adopting its culture, so the answer is moderate.

religious-nation.rationale: Savarkar insists Hindutva is wider than a creed (Sikhs, Jains and Lingayats are Hindus by blood and culture) and Golwalkar says change of worship does not make one an alien; the nation is defined by land, descent and culture, not by religion alone.

nation-first.rationale: Savarkar urges Hindus to consolidate the Indian nation first while other peoples organise on narrow racial or religious bases, and Golwalkar writes that nationalism cannot be destroyed and that the UN has failed to harmonise national ambitions.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Savarkar holds that Hindus, with the Gita and Buddha behind them, could dictate terms to the world, and Golwalkar's opening chapters give Hindu society a unique world mission as 'final refuge for mankind'; neither treats cultures as merely different.

communal-electorates.rationale: Savarkar (1923) says communities may press for communal representation if they find it indispensable, while Golwalkar and the RSS demand an end to separate electorates and talk of 'minorities'.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Golwalkar says Partition is not a settled fact and that 'we are here to unsettle it', and Jaffrelot records the RSS Pratinidhi Sabha's 1959 and 1965 pledges to Akhand Bharat.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Golwalkar protests India's failure to answer atrocities on Hindus in East Bengal, and the RSS's 2025 ABPS resolution urges India to stand with and protect Bangladesh's Hindus.

traditional-family.rationale: Golwalkar makes the home and mothers the centre of national samskars, and the RSS's 2019 ABPS resolution calls the Hindu family the basic unit linking the individual to the nation and urges efforts to sustain it.

national-rebirth.rationale: Savarkar urges consolidating a Hindu people that has not yet used its strength, and Golwalkar writes of rejuvenating Hindu Rashtra and a virile national life; neither speaks of a radical break.

racial-pride.rationale: Savarkar celebrates the Hindu race and its blood and Golwalkar's We calls for glorification of the Hindu race and culture and cites race pride as a model.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Savarkar calls on Hindus to organise in defence of their race and land and Golwalkar's Sangh does the same, with 'race' meaning the Hindu people.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Savarkar praises commingling of the Hindu races and wants intermarriage between provinces and castes encouraged, while Golwalkar's We cites Germany's race purity as a lesson.

notes: Searched all themes: economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means. Golwalkar's views on economics, women's roles, caste and most governance questions are his own and are left null under the strand rule (also his conversion, cow, unitary-state, communism, minorities and war positions). His 1939 text and his 1966 book differ on minorities' civic rights; the later book is used as the mature position and the RSS has since distanced itself from the earlier one. Savarkar's other writings (e.g. Hindu Rashtra Darshan) and Upadhyaya's Integral Humanism were not read.
